The low-pressure T106C turbine blade is characterized by a high degree of camber, with sharp leading and trailing edges and a maximum blade thickness at the 35% chord length location.

The high-pressure C3X turbine blade is characterized by a very thick leading edge with a maximum thickness at the 5% chord length location, a sharp trailing edge, and 10 circular penetrating cooling channels.
The blades were subjected to a centrifugal load of 109.3 kN and a pressure difference of 316 kPa across the blade.
Grade 310 Stainless Steel was used as the blade material in this study.
A mesh dependency study was conducted, and 50,000 linear hexahedral (C3D8R) finite elements were used to discretize the blade geometries.
The SIMP optimization for the T106C blade converged after 32 iterations, reducing the compliance by 41.6% compared to the original 50% volume structure.
The SERA optimization for the T106C blade converged after 57 iterations, reducing the compliance by 36.7% compared to the original 50% volume structure.
The SIMP optimization for the C3X blade converged after 28 iterations, reducing the compliance by 33.6% compared to the original 50% volume structure.
The SERA optimization for the C3X blade converged after 91 iterations, reducing the compliance by 22.0% compared to the original 50% volume structure.

The SIMP-derived topologies were characterized by smooth boundaries and an even material distribution across the camber line, while the SERA-derived topologies were composed of intricate features with unrealistic connectivity.
The SERA method was less computationally efficient, consistently requiring about 2.6 times longer than SIMP to achieve convergence.

The hypothesis proposed was that the differences between the SIMP and SERA optimization results were caused by the application of a mesh smoothing filter in the ATOM SIMP optimization, which decreased structural performance for increased manufacturability.
The open-source SERA optimization algorithm was modified to allow the definition of non-designable regions, expanding its capability to geometrically constrained problems.
The optimized T106C blade design consisted of a thin cavity, centered around the camber line, extending from the blade root to the blade tip.
The optimized C3X blade design was a hollow geometry, with material reinforcements around the channel boundaries and at high-stress locations along the blade skin.
